prompt: Ana runs `go vet ./...` in her module and sees nothing at all, then `echo $?` prints `0`. What does that tell her?
hint: Vet prints only when it has something to report.

choices.text: No analyzer reported anything in any package
choices.why: Right. A clean run is silent and exits 0, which is what lets a script read only the exit code.

choices.text: Vet skipped the packages because none of them has tests
choices.why: Vet reads source, not tests; lesson 1's `hits` was vetted package by package, `tools/genlog` included.

choices.text: The module is free of bugs
choices.why: Vet looks for a few dozen classes of mistake. A clean run says none of those is present, and section 05 shows a crash it passed.

choices.text: Only the package in the current directory was checked
choices.why: `./...` means every package under the current directory, not only the one in it.

prompt: `fmt.Printf("%d%%\n", share)` with `share` a `float64` compiles and prints `%!d(float64=9.365)%`. Why did the compiler accept it?
hint: Look at the parameter types of `Printf`.

choices.text: The compiler converts the float to an integer when the verb asks for one
choices.why: Nothing was converted: the output shows `fmt` receiving a `float64` and refusing to print it as `%d`.

choices.text: To it the format is a string and the arguments are `...any`
choices.why: Right. Any argument of any type is legal; only something that knows what `fmt` does with the string can compare the two, and that is vet.

choices.text: Format checking is turned off unless the build uses `-gcflags`
choices.why: There is no compiler flag for it; the check lives in vet's `printf` analyzer.

choices.text: `%d` is accepted for floats in Go, and only rounds them
choices.why: If it were, the program would have printed `9`. It printed `%!d(float64=9.365)`, `fmt`'s sign of a wrong verb.

prompt: Each proposed check below was turned down for vet. Match it with the criterion from `cmd/vet/README` that it fails.
hint: Correctness, frequency, precision: one each.

pairs.left: a check that flags exported functions with no doc comment
a check for a real bug found in a handful of programs anywhere
a check whose warnings are wrong often enough that people stop reading them

prompt: A team upgrades its machines to Go 1.27.1 but leaves `go 1.21` in `go.mod`. A goroutine started in a `for` loop reads the loop variable. What does `go vet` do, and is the program wrong?
hint: Which file decides the loop semantics?

choices.text: Vet is silent and the program is correct, because the toolchain is 1.27.1
choices.why: The toolchain gives each file the semantics its module declares. `oldloop` under `go 1.21` printed `/health` three times.

choices.text: Vet reports `loop variable captured by func literal`, and the bug is real
choices.why: Right. The `go` line keeps the old shared-variable loop, so the bug exists, and `loopclosure` reports it because the file declares a Go older than 1.22.

choices.text: Vet refuses to run until `go.mod` matches the toolchain
choices.why: A module declaring an older Go builds and vets normally under a newer toolchain; only a newer `go` line fails with `GOTOOLCHAIN=local`.

choices.text: Vet reports it, but the warning is a false alarm on 1.27.1
choices.why: The warning matches what the program does: under `go 1.21` all goroutines see the last value.

prompt: `counter`'s `Add` has the receiver `(c Counter)`, and `Counter` holds a `sync.Mutex` and a map. Why did eight goroutines crash it with `concurrent map writes`?
hint: What does each call get, and what do the copies share?

choices.text: `sync.Mutex` cannot be used inside a struct with a map
choices.why: A mutex beside the map it guards is the usual shape; it works as long as everyone locks the same mutex.

choices.text: Each call locks its own copy of the mutex, while every copy shares one map
choices.why: Right. The value receiver copies the struct; the copied map value still refers to the same table, so the writes collide with no lock between them.

choices.text: `wg.Go` starts goroutines before `Add` returns
choices.why: `wg.Go` only schedules the function; the crash comes from the writes inside `Add`, not from when goroutines start.

choices.text: The `defer` unlocks the mutex before the map is written
choices.why: A deferred call runs when the function returns, after `c.n[path]++`.

prompt: The tag on `Hits` was written `json: "hits"`, with a space after the colon. What did `encoding/json` do with the field?
hint: A tag it cannot parse is treated as no tag.

choices.text: Refused to encode and returned an error
choices.why: Nothing failed: `Encode` wrote the array. That is why the bug survives.

choices.text: Wrote it as `"hits"` anyway, ignoring the space
choices.why: The output shows `"Hits":2576`; the tag was not read at all.

choices.text: Left the field out of the output
choices.why: It is there, under another name.

choices.text: Wrote it under its Go name, `Hits`
choices.why: Right. `reflect.StructTag.Get` gave up on the malformed tag, so the field kept its Go name, and a client reading `hits` reads nothing.

prompt: `length` in `header` is fixed to `return uint16(hi)<<8 | uint16(lo)`. What does `length([]byte{0x02, 0x10})` return now?
hint: 0x0210 in decimal: the high byte times 256, plus the low byte.

prompt: Match each message `go vet` printed with the analyzer that wrote it.
hint: Each analyzer is named after the mistake it looks for.

pairs.left: `the cancel function is not used on all paths (possible context leak)`
`hi (8 bits) too small for shift of 8`

prompt: `go test ./status` printed two vet messages and `FAIL example.com/vetted/status [build failed]`. How many of the package's tests ran?
hint: Where does `go test` put the vet step?

choices.text: All of them, and vet's messages were printed afterwards
choices.why: Vet runs before the test binary; with a finding, the binary is never run.

choices.text: Only `TestParse`, since the other one is misnamed
choices.why: That is what `-vet=off` did. With vet on, nothing ran at all.

choices.text: None
choices.why: Right. The go command treats vet as part of building the test binary, and a vet finding stops the build, so no test runs.

choices.text: Every test except the ones in the file vet complained about
choices.why: Vet's finding fails the whole package's build, whichever file it is in.

prompt: On Go 1.27.1, how many vet analyzers does `go test` run by default, counting from the list compiled into the go command?
hint: The help text names one fewer than the source does.

prompt: With `-vet=off`, `go test -v ./status` printed `--- PASS: TestParse` and `ok`. What did that green line hide?
hint: Count the tests in the file and the tests in the output.

choices.text: A test that never ran, and the range bug it would have caught
choices.why: Right. `TestparseRejects` is not a test name `testing` recognises, so it was skipped in silence, and it was the test that finds `Parse` accepting `600`.

choices.text: Nothing: vet's findings were style, and the tests are what count
choices.why: Neither finding was style: one was a test that never runs, the other an `errors.As` call that panics when reached.

choices.text: A cached result from an earlier run
choices.why: The cache was cleared before the run, and a cached result says `(cached)` on the `ok` line.

choices.text: A panic in `TestParse` that `-vet=off` swallowed
choices.why: `-vet=off` removes the vet step and nothing else; `TestParse` passed for real.

prompt: `go test ./counter` passed although `counter` copies a mutex. To make that same command run every analyzer, Ana adds `-vet=___`.
hint: The opposite of `off`.

prompt: What does `go vet -printf=false ./...` run?
hint: Turning one analyzer off leaves the rest on.

choices.text: Only the `printf` analyzer, with its wrapper inference off
choices.why: That would be selecting `printf`. `=false` excludes it.

choices.text: Every analyzer except `printf`
choices.why: Right. Turning one off with `-NAME=false` runs all the others; naming one with `-NAME` runs only the ones named.

choices.text: Nothing: one `=false` turns the whole suite off
choices.why: The two programs whose only bug was a `printf` one passed, and `counter` would still have failed.

choices.text: The twelve analyzers `go test` uses, minus `printf`
choices.why: `go vet` does not use `go test`'s list; it starts from all 35.

prompt: `logf` calls `fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "applog: "+format+"\n", args...)`, and vet did not check its callers. What is the fix that needs no flag?
hint: Look at how `warnf` was written.

choices.text: Rename it `Logf`, since vet checks exported names
choices.why: Vet inferred the unexported `warnf` as a wrapper; the name is not what decides.

choices.text: Move it into a package of its own
choices.why: Wrappers are inferred within a package and across packages alike; the concatenated format is what hides it.

choices.text: Format with `fmt.Sprintf(format, args...)` first, then add the prefix
choices.why: Right. Passing `format` and `args...` straight to a known formatter makes it a wrapper vet recognises, as `warnf` is.

choices.text: Add a doc comment that says it takes a format
choices.why: Vet does not read doc comments to decide what a function is.

prompt: Which of these does `go vet`, as it ships, never report? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them were shown failing vet in section 03.

choices.text: A variable declared again with `:=` inside an `if`, hiding the outer one
choices.why: Yes. `load` did exactly that, vet passed it, and only the separate `shadow` analyzer named the line.

choices.text: An unexported function nothing calls
choices.why: Yes. It is legal and often deliberate, so it fails the correctness criterion; that is lesson 8's ground.

choices.text: `l.limit = l.limit`
choices.why: `assign` reports it: `self-assignment of l.limit`.

choices.text: A statement after a `return` in the same block
choices.why: `unreachable` reports it, as it did in `limit`.

prompt: To run an installed analysis tool in place of vet's own suite, Ana types `go vet -___=$(command -v shadow) ./load`.
hint: The flag names the program vet should run.

prompt: Put in order what happens when `go test ./status` runs on a package with no mistakes.
hint: The vet step belongs to building the test binary.
items: the compiler type-checks the package and its test files
the twelve default analyzers run over the same code
the test binary is built and run

prompt: A service's `Stats` type holds a `sync.RWMutex`, and its `Snapshot` method has a value receiver. The CI pipeline runs only `go test ./...`, whose tests call `Snapshot` from one goroutine. What does the pipeline report?
hint: Which analyzers does `go test` run by default?

choices.text: A `copylocks` failure, since every vet finding fails `go test`
choices.why: Only the default subset fails a test run, and `copylocks` is not in it; `counter` passed `go test` the same way.

choices.text: Green, and the copied lock ships
choices.why: Right. `copylocks` is outside `go test`'s twelve and one goroutine never races with itself. A `go vet ./...` step, or `-vet=all`, would have failed.

choices.text: A compile error, because a mutex cannot be copied
choices.why: Copying a struct with a mutex is legal Go; that is why vet exists for it.

choices.text: A data race report from the test run
choices.why: Races are reported by the race detector, with `-race`, and only when two goroutines actually meet.

prompt: `type Timeout struct{}` has `func (e *Timeout) Error() string`, with a pointer receiver. Which wrap does vet's `%w` check report, in a module declaring `go 1.27.1`?
hint: Which type implements `error` here: `Timeout` or `*Timeout`?

choices.text: `fmt.Errorf("read: %w", &Timeout{})`
choices.why: With a pointer receiver the error type is `*Timeout`, so wrapping `&Timeout{}` is the right operand.

choices.text: Neither: `%w` is only checked for value receivers
choices.why: The check is about the operand not being an error, which `Timeout{}` is not here; `printf` reports that too.

choices.text: Both, because `%w` always wants a value
choices.why: `%w` wants the type that implements `error`; for a pointer receiver that is the pointer.

choices.text: `fmt.Errorf("read: %w", Timeout{})`
choices.why: Right. Only `*Timeout` has the `Error` method, so `Timeout{}` is not an error at all; `notfound` was the mirror case, a value receiver wrapped as a pointer.

prompt: `fetch` printed `<nil>` and `no path to fetch`, both correct, and vet still failed it with `lostcancel`. What does the bug cost?
hint: What does `cancel` release, and when is it released without it?

choices.text: The wrong answer on the early return
choices.why: The early return printed the right error; the output was correct on both paths.

choices.text: A goroutine that never exits
choices.why: The context's timer fires after two seconds and releases it; nothing is stuck for ever.

choices.text: A context and its timer, held two seconds on every early return
choices.why: Right. Without `cancel` they live until the timeout fires; at thousands of calls a second that is memory growing with traffic.

choices.text: A panic when the parent context is cancelled
choices.why: Cancelling a parent cancels its children quietly; nothing panics.
